segments.text: This demo compares SHA-3-256, the compact core in this project, and Oxide's quartz implementation.
Here's how the input architecture changes speed and resource use.

chapters.title: A shared stream, then the Quartz core

segments.text: Start at the input. Both cores receive the same 64-bit AXI stream.
That stream can come from the processing system, Ethernet ingress, or the block RAM replay reader.
In the Quartz integration, a local adapter feeds one byte per clock into two full block buffers.
One fills, while the other feeds the hash state.
24 permutation rounds produce the result, which is copied into a separate digest register.

chapters.title: Compact: absorb directly into the state

segments.text: The compact core uses that same stream interface.
It captures up to 8 bytes at a time, then absorbs them directly into the hash state with an aligned exclusive OR.
The two full block buffers disappear.
The digest comes directly from the held state, so that separate register disappears too.
Capture and absorption still take separate cycles.
The 24-round permutation is unchanged.
Two smaller changes simplify the compact core further.
First, padding.
Compare this project's earlier wide core with the compact version.
Previously, a variable index selected from all 25 state lanes.
The compact version decodes the destination locally,
across only the 17 rate lanes that padding can touch.
The eight capacity lanes remain in the hash state.
Padding leaves them alone.
Second, input validation.
The earlier design checked the byte mask and end of message flag on the state update control
path.
The compact core records that check while capturing the input.
On the next cycle, a bad word is rejected before absorption.
These changes reduce surrounding logic.
They preserve the hash algorithm and the simulated cycle count.
This experiment compares SHA-3 256 in the compact core with Oxide's quartz implementation.
The input comes from block RAM, memory built into the FPGA.
That lets the comparison focus on the hardware hashing path.
A small, repeatable pattern is loaded once.
The FPGA reads it, returns to the beginning, and keeps the stream moving.
The hash state continues across every pass.
A small memory can therefore supply one large, continuous message.
The hardware timer starts with the hash job and stops when the digest is ready.
Loading the pattern happens before timing begins.
The measurement includes the memory reader, framing, and the selected hash core.
Both cores use the same board, the same memory path, and a 100 MHz clock.
Messages start at 64 bytes and double at each step, across 25 sizes.
Seven measured runs follow warm-up at every size.
That's 350 measured hashes in this replay experiment.

chapters.title: Start the real GUI sweep; 32x fast-forward

segments.text: Now run that experiment in HashLab, check the connected board, then start the sweep.
Each progress bar counts completed hashes for one implementation.
The cores take turns on the same FPGA. They aren't running in parallel.
This part of the recording is sped up, while the measurements still come
from the hardware cycle counter. When the sweep finishes, open the results.
For the largest message, about 1,074 megabytes,
Quartz takes 10.737 seconds.
The compact core takes 4.5.
The input is identical.
Both implementations produce the same digest.
Now follow the throughput as the messages grow.
Oxide's quartz settles at about 100 megabytes per second.
The compact core reaches 238.6.
Once the messages are large, both curves settle into a steady rate.
The speed up is quartz's time divided by the compact core's time.
One means equal speed.
For large messages, the compact core reaches about 2.4 times the throughput.
That advantage stays as the message keeps growing.
The compact hash partition also uses fewer resources, 21.9% fewer lookup tables, and about 58% fewer flip-flops.
The replay memory is shared infrastructure, counted separately from those hash partition totals.
